Construction started in 1997 under Michel Guyot, owner of Château de Saint-Fargeau, a castle in Saint-Fargeau 13 kilometres (8.1 mi) away. The site was chosen according to the availability of construction materials: an abandoned stone quarry, in a large forest, with a nearby pond. [...] In 1979, French entrepreneur Michel Guyot purchased the ruins of the Château de Saint-Fargeau and began restoring it [...] A former sandstone quarry was chosen as the site of Guédelon Castle because of its relative elevation and abundance of local natural resources, which would have been expensive to transport in the Middle Ages. The castle location is in a woodland, two hours south of Paris, near Treigny. The ceremonial first stone was laid on 20 June 1997 [...] By 1998 the castle perimeter had been built up to a metre (3 ¼ feet) in height, following which Guédelon was opened to the public. By June 2010, the great tower stood at 15 metres (49 ft). By 2014, the castle was attracting about 300,000 visitors annually [...] The techniques redeveloped for Guédelon Castle were used in the reconstruction of Notre-Dame cathedral in Paris after its catastrophic 2019 fire. [...] the project was described as "the world's biggest archaeological experiment". [...] explored the use of medieval treadmill cranes in its construction.

gancho: A Tapeçaria de Bayeux nem é tapeçaria: é um bordado de quase 70 metros. Na Segunda Guerra, Himmler a cobiçou, e a SS foi buscá-la no Louvre quando o museu já estava de novo em mãos francesas.
explicacao: Numa tapeçaria verdadeira, a imagem é tecida no próprio pano. Na de Bayeux, as figuras foram bordadas com fio de lã sobre um linho grosso, com quatro tipos de ponto e dez cores de tintas naturais. Ela tem cerca de 50 centímetros de altura e conta, em 58 cenas, os fatos que levaram à conquista normanda da Inglaterra e à Batalha de Hastings, em 1066. Há 623 figuras humanas, 994 animais e 41 navios e barcos, além da primeira imagem conhecida do cometa Halley. As cenas finais se perderam. Em geral se acredita que foi encomendada pelo bispo Odo de Bayeux, meio-irmão de Guilherme, o Conquistador, e feita na Inglaterra nos anos seguintes à conquista. Durante a ocupação alemã da França, Heinrich Himmler a considerava importante para a história germânica. Em 27 de junho de 1944, a Gestapo a levou ao Louvre, e em 18 de agosto Himmler mandou transferi-la para "um lugar seguro", provavelmente Berlim, numa mensagem interceptada em Bletchley Park. A SS só tentou pegá-la em 22 de agosto, tarde demais. Em setembro de 2026, a obra saiu da França pela primeira vez, emprestada ao Museu Britânico.

fontes.trecho: The Bayeux Tapestry (French: Tapisserie de Bayeux) is an embroidered cloth nearly 70 metres (230 feet) long and 50 centimetres (20 inches) tall that depicts the events leading up to the Norman conquest of England, led by William, Duke of Normandy, and the Battle of Hastings in 1066. [...] Despite its name, the work is technically an embroidery rather than a true tapestry, since the images are stitched rather than woven into the fabric. It was worked in wool thread on a coarse linen ground using four different stitches and ten natural dye colours. The cloth now consists of 58 scenes, all with Medieval Latin tituli. The surviving piece depicts 623 human figures, 994 animals, 438 plants, 37 buildings and fortifications, 41 ships and boats [...] The final scenes are missing. [...] It is generally thought to have been commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, William's half-brother who appears four times, and produced in England in the years following the Conquest. [...] In September 2026 the tapestry travelled outside France for the first time in its history, on loan to the British Museum [...] The picture of Halley's Comet, which appears in the upper border at (scene 32), is also the first known picture of this comet. [...] during the German occupation of France and the Normandy landings. During the war Heinrich Himmler coveted the work, regarding it as "important for our glorious and cultured Germanic history". [...] On 27 June 1944 the Gestapo took the tapestry to the Louvre, and on 18 August, three days before the Wehrmacht withdrew from Paris, Himmler sent a message (intercepted by Bletchley Park) ordering it to be taken to "a place of safety", thought to be Berlin. It was only on 22 August that the SS attempted to take possession of the tapestry, by which time the Louvre was again in French hands.

gancho: O Domesday Book, levantamento da Inglaterra de 1086, ainda está guardado e legível. Sua versão digital, feita pela BBC em 1986 em laserdiscs, preocupava já em 2002: quase não sobravam máquinas para lê-la.
explicacao: Em 1085, Guilherme, o Conquistador, mandou agentes a cada condado para listar terras, gente, gado e o que cada propriedade rendia ao seu senhor, e o colofão do livro diz que o levantamento terminou em 1086. O manuscrito em pergaminho está hoje nos Arquivos Nacionais, em Kew, Londres. O nome é uma alusão ao Juízo Final: por volta de 1179, Richard FitzNeal escreveu que as decisões do livro eram inalteráveis, como as do Juízo Final, e que sua sentença não podia ser anulada. Para os 900 anos, a BBC e parceiros criaram um novo Domesday multimídia, publicado em 1986, com textos sobre a vida local escritos sobretudo por crianças de mais de 9 mil escolas, além de mapas, fotos, vídeos e o censo de 1981. Tudo foi gravado em laserdiscs adaptados, que só funcionavam num computador BBC Master ligado a um toca-discos especial da Philips. Em 2002, surgiu o temor de que os discos ficassem ilegíveis, porque computadores e leitores capazes de usá-los tinham ficado raros. Um projeto das universidades de Leeds e de Michigan conseguiu resgatar o conteúdo por emulação. O caso virou exemplo clássico de obsolescência digital.

fontes.trecho: The BBC Domesday Project was a partnership between Acorn Computers, Philips, Logica, and the BBC (with some funding from the European Commission's ESPRIT programme) to mark the 900th anniversary of the original Domesday Book, an 11th-century census of England. It has been cited as an example of digital obsolescence on account of the physical medium used for data storage. This new multimedia edition of Domesday was compiled between 1984 and 1986 and published in 1986. It included a new "survey" of the United Kingdom, in which people, mostly school children, wrote about geography, history or social issues in their local area or just about their daily lives. This was linked with maps, and many colour photos, statistical data, video and "virtual walks". The project also incorporated professionally prepared video footage, virtual reality tours of major landmarks and other prepared datasets such as the 1981 census. Over a million people participated in the project, including children from more than 9,000 schools. [...] The project was stored on adapted LaserDiscs [...] Viewing the discs required the BBC Master AIV, a Acorn BBC Master computer expanded with a SCSI controller and the 65C102 "Turbo" co-processor - which controlled a Philips VP415 LaserVision laserdisc player. [...] In 2002, concerns emerged over the potential unreadablility of the discs as computers capable of reading the format became rare and drives capable of accessing the discs even rarer. [...] the CAMiLEON project (a partnership between the University of Leeds and University of Michigan, led by Margaret Hedstrom and managed by researcher Paul Wheatley) had developed a system capable of accessing the discs using emulation techniques.

at the behest of William the Conqueror [...] The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle states that in 1085 the king sent his agents to survey every shire in England, to list his holdings and dues owed to him. [...] The survey's main purpose was to record the annual value of every piece of landed property to its lord, and the resources in land, labour force, and livestock from which the value derived. [...] Richard FitzNeal wrote in the Dialogus de Scaccario (c. 1179) that the book was so called because its decisions were unalterable, like those of the Last Judgment, and its sentence could not be quashed. The manuscript is now held at the National Archives in Kew, London. [...] the book's colophon states the survey was completed in 1086. [...] copied out by one person on parchment (prepared sheepskin)

gancho: Na Idade Média, corria que certos gansos nasciam de cracas presas em madeira à deriva no mar. O imperador Frederico II mandou buscar essas madeiras no norte para examinar e não viu nelas nada parecido com uma ave.
explicacao: As cracas-pescoço-de-ganso, presas a troncos boiando, têm um pedúnculo comprido que lembra o pescoço de uma ave, e o ganso-de-faces-brancas nunca era visto fazendo ninho na Europa. A lenda juntou as duas coisas. Por volta de 1188, o clérigo Geraldo de Gales escreveu que essas aves nasciam em madeira de abeto à deriva, cresciam presas pelo bico dentro de conchas e um dia caíam na água ou voavam, e garantiu ter visto com os próprios olhos mais de mil embriões pendurados num só pedaço de madeira. Os bestiários, copiados em mosteiros, espalharam a história. Frederico II, imperador e estudioso de aves, fez o contrário: no tratado sobre caça com aves que escreveu por volta de 1241, contou que enviou emissários ao norte para trazer as tais madeiras e que as formações parecidas com conchas não lembravam em nada o corpo de uma ave. Para ele, a lenda nasceu porque esses gansos se reproduzem em lugares tão remotos que ninguém sabia onde faziam ninho. Hoje se sabe que esses gansos migram para se reproduzir no extremo norte, como na Groenlândia e no norte da Escandinávia. Conta-se ainda que o papa Inocêncio III proibiu, em 1215, comer esses gansos na Quaresma como se não fossem carne, mas as atas do concílio não registram essa proibição.

fontes.trecho: The barnacle goose myth is a widely reported historical misconception about the breeding habits of the barnacle goose (Branta leucopsis) and brant goose (Branta bernicla). One version of the myth is that these geese emerge fully formed from goose barnacles (Cirripedia). [...] The main vector for the myth into modern times was monastic manuscripts and in particular the bestiary. The myth owes its long-standing popularity to an early ignorance of the migration patterns of geese. [...] It was not until the late 19th century that bird migration research showed that such geese migrate northwards to nest and breed in Greenland or northern Scandinavia. [...] whilst in the curvature of its stalk they saw a resemblance to the long neck of the bird. [...] Topographia Hibernica, compiled by Gerald of Wales around 1188. [...] there are many birds called barnacles (bernacae) … nature produces them in a marvellous way for they are born at first in gum-like form from fir-wood adrift in the sea. Then they cling by their beaks like sea-wood, sticking to wood, enclosed in a shell-fish shells for freer development … thus in the process of time dressed in a firm clothing of feathers, they either fall into the waters or fly off into freedom of the air. [...] Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II   (1194–1250), an ornithologist and learned scholar, is best remembered  for his seminal work, De Arte Venandi cum Avibus (On the Art of Hunting With Birds). This book was written in Latin around the year 1241. [...] I have often seen with my own eyes more than a thousand minute embryos of birds of this species on the seashore, hanging from one piece of timber, covered with shells, and, already formed. [...] We have made prolonged research into the origin and truth of this legend and even sent special envoys to the north with order to bring back specimens of these mythical timbers for our inspection. When we examined them we did observe shell-like formations clinging to the rotten wood, but these bore no resemblance to any avian body. We therefor doubt the truth of this legend in the absence of corroborative evidence. In our opinion this superstition arose from the fact that barnacle geese breed in such remote latitudes that men in ignorance of their real nesting places invented this explanation. [...] considered it necessary in 1215 to prohibit the eating of barnacle geese in Lent [...] However the records of the 4th Lateran Council do not include reference to such a ban amongst any of its decisions.

gancho: Por séculos, o Tesouro inglês registrou impostos e dívidas em varetas de madeira entalhadas. Abolido o sistema, mandaram queimá-las em fornalhas do Parlamento, em 1834. O fogo escapou e destruiu a maior parte do prédio.
explicacao: O sistema foi introduzido na Inglaterra por Henrique I, por volta de 1100, numa época de pouca moeda. Cada valor virava um entalhe numa vareta de aveleira, e a largura do corte dizia o montante: a largura da palma da mão valia mil libras, a de um polegar, cem, a do dedo mínimo, vinte, e um grão de cevada inchado marcava uma libra. Depois a vareta era rachada ao meio no sentido do comprimento, e cada parte ficava com uma metade. Como as irregularidades da madeira rachada só deixavam as duas metades originais se encaixarem, era quase impossível fraudar: um entalhe a mais numa metade não apareceria na outra. As varetas registravam impostos pagos, mas logo passaram a circular como "dinheiro de madeira", aceitas com desconto como pagamento. Em 1697, o recém-criado Banco da Inglaterra emitiu ações em troca de varetas da dívida da Coroa. O Tesouro só abandonou o método em 1826. Em 1834, seis séculos de registros foram queimados em duas fornalhas do Parlamento, a chaminé pegou fogo e o incêndio se espalhou até destruir a maior parte do edifício. Charles Dickens contou o episódio num artigo de 1855.

fontes.trecho: The split tally became a prevalent technique in medieval Europe, a time characterised by a scarcity of coinage, to document bilateral exchanges and debts. Typically fashioned from squared hazelwood, the stick was inscribed with a series of notches before being split lengthwise. Each party in the transaction retained one half of the marked stick, both pieces bearing identical records. [...] The natural irregularities in the surfaces of the tallies where they were split would mean that only the original two halves would fit back together perfectly, and so would verify that they were matching halves of the same transaction. If one party tried to unilaterally change the value of his half of the tally stick by adding more notches, the absence of those notches would be apparent on the other party's tally stick. [...] when Henry I introduced the tally stick system in medieval England in around 1100. The tally sticks recorded a payment of taxes, but soon began to circulate in a secondary discount market, being accepted as payment for goods and services at a discount [...] and circulated as "wooden money". [...] At the top of the tally a cut is made, the thickness of the palm of the hand, to represent a thousand pounds; then a hundred pounds by a cut the breadth of a thumb; twenty pounds, the breadth of the little finger; a single pound, the width of a swollen barleycorn [...] Royal tallies (debt of the Crown) also played a role in the formation of the Bank of England at the end of the 17th century. In 1697, the bank issued £1 million worth of stock in exchange for £800,000 worth of tallies at par [...] The split tally of the Exchequer remained in continuous use in England until 1826 [...] In 1834, following the passing of 4 Will. 4. c .15, tally sticks representing six centuries' worth of financial records were ordered to be burned in two furnaces in the Houses of Parliament. The resulting fire set the chimney ablaze and then spread until most of the building was destroyed. This event was described by Charles Dickens in an 1855 article on administrative reform.

gancho: Na Idade Média, havia quem se fechasse para sempre numa cela colada à parede de uma igreja. Na entrada, rezava-se um rito parecido com um funeral, e a pessoa passava a ser tida como morta para o mundo.
explicacao: Eram os anacoretas. Diferentemente dos eremitas, faziam voto de ficar num lugar só, e a cela costumava ser um cômodo simples encostado à igreja da aldeia. Em terras de língua germânica, desde pelo menos o século X, o bispo rezava o Ofício dos Mortos quando o recluso entrava, e às vezes, se a pessoa era emparedada, punha seu selo na parede. A cela tinha em geral no máximo 3,7 a 4,6 metros de lado e três janelinhas: uma dava para o altar, para acompanhar a missa e receber a comunhão; outra servia a quem trazia comida e levava os dejetos; a terceira deixava entrar luz. Pela janela, os anacoretas aconselhavam visitantes e ganhavam fama de sábios. O compromisso era tão sério que alguns se recusaram a sair nem quando piratas ou saqueadores atacaram a cidade, e morreram queimados quando a igreja foi incendiada. Na Inglaterra, chegaram a cerca de 200 no século XIII, e as mulheres eram maioria, às vezes quatro para cada homem. Uma delas, Juliana de Norwich, morta depois de 1416, escreveu o texto místico Revelações do Amor Divino. A tradição inglesa acabou com o fechamento dos mosteiros por Henrique VIII, entre 1536 e 1539.

fontes.trecho: Anchorites are frequently considered to be a type of hermit, but unlike hermits, they were required to take a vow of stability of place, opting for permanent enclosure in cells often attached to churches. Also unlike hermits, anchorites were subject to a religious rite of consecration that closely resembled the funeral rite, following which they would be considered dead to the world and a type of living saint. [...] Their highest number—around 200 anchorites—was recorded in the 13th century. From the 12th to the 16th centuries, female anchorites consistently outnumbered their male counterparts, sometimes by as many as four to one in the 13th century. [...] Between 1536 and 1539, the dissolution of the monasteries ordered by Henry VIII of England effectively brought the anchorite tradition to an end in England. [...] They tended to be a simple cell (also called anchorhold) built against one of the walls of the local village church. In Germanic-speaking areas, from at least the tenth century it was customary for the bishop to say the Office of the Dead as the anchorite entered their cell, to signify the anchorite's death to the world [...] Sometimes, if the anchorite was walled up inside the cell, the bishop would put his seal upon the wall to stamp it with his authority. [...] Most anchorholds were small, perhaps at most 3.7 to 4.6 m (12 to 15 ft) square, with three windows. Viewing the altar, hearing Mass, and receiving the Eucharist were possible through one small, shuttered window in the common wall facing the sanctuary [...] Anchorites provided spiritual advice and counsel to visitors through these windows, gaining a reputation for wisdom. Another small window allowed access to those who saw to the anchorite's physical needs. A third window, often facing the street but covered with translucent cloth, allowed light into the cell. [...] Some refused to leave their cells even when pirates or looters were pillaging their towns and consequently burned to death when the church was torched. [...] providing food and water and removing waste. [...] Julian of Norwich (died after 1416) wrote the mystic text Revelations of Divine Love

gancho: Os primeiros relógios mecânicos das torres da Europa muitas vezes não tinham mostrador nem ponteiros: só tocavam sino nas horas de oração. Por isso clock, relógio em inglês, vem de clocca, sino em latim medieval.
explicacao: O avanço decisivo foi o escape de verga, um mecanismo que libera a força de um peso aos poucos e tornou possíveis os primeiros relógios mecânicos, por volta de 1300. Entre 1280 e 1320, os registros de igrejas passam a citar relógios com mais frequência, o que provavelmente indica a chegada desse novo tipo. Os relógios mais simples, feitos para avisar, ficavam em torres e anunciavam as horas canônicas, os horários de oração, que mudavam de duração conforme o nascer e o pôr do sol. Por isso dispensavam mostrador. O nome conta essa história: em inglês, clock vem do latim medieval clocca, sino, e tem parentes em várias línguas europeias, como o holandês médio clocke. Um exemplo que sobreviveu é o relógio da Catedral de Salisbury, na Inglaterra, de ferro forjado e sem mostrador, que se acredita ser de cerca de 1386. Movido por dois grandes pesos de pedra, ele serve para tocar um sino na hora certa. É chamado de relógio mais antigo do mundo ainda funcionando, mas há dúvidas sobre a data, e outros relógios reivindicam o título.

fontes.trecho: The word clock derives from the medieval Latin word for 'bell'—clocca—and has cognates in many European languages. [...] Middle Dutch clocke, all of which mean 'bell'. [...] In Europe, between 1280 and 1320, there was an increase in the number of references to clocks and horologes in church records, and this probably indicates that a ne [...] Simple clocks intended mainly for notification were installed in towers and did not always require faces or hands. They would have announced the canonical hours or intervals between set times of prayer. Canonical hours varied in length as the times of sunrise and sunset shifted. [...] A major advance occurred with the invention of the verge escapement, which made possible the first mechanical clocks around 1300 in Europe [...] This controlled release of power – the escapement – marks the beginning of the true mechanical clock

The Salisbury Cathedral clock is a large iron-framed tower clock without a dial, in Salisbury Cathedral, England. Thought to date from about 1386, it is a well-preserved example of the earliest type of mechanical clock, called verge and foliot clocks, and is said to be the oldest working clock in the world, although similar claims are made for other clocks. [...] Like many of these more practical devices, its main purpose was to strike a bell at precise times. It probably did not have a dial. The wheels and gears are mounted in a four-post wrought iron frame. [...] The power was supplied by two large stone weights. [...] There are some doubts that the clock displayed in Salisbury Cathedral is actually the clock mentioned in 1386

gancho: Expectativa de vida de uns 30 anos na Idade Média não significa que adultos morriam aos 30: as mortes de bebês puxavam a média para baixo, e quem chegava aos 30 morria, em média, entre os 50 e os 60.
explicacao: A confusão vem da expectativa de vida ao nascer, uma média que inclui todos os que morrem, até os bebês. Em todas as sociedades antes da era moderna, a idade em que mais gente morria era o primeiro ano de vida. Quando a mortalidade infantil é alta, essa média fica muito sensível às mortes dos primeiros anos e engana: numa sociedade com expectativa de vida ao nascer de 40 anos, poucos morrem exatamente aos 40, e a maioria morre antes dos 30 ou depois dos 55. Além da mortalidade infantil, mortes de jovens adultos por acidentes, epidemias, guerras e partos também baixavam a média. Por isso, demógrafos usam outras medidas, como a expectativa de vida aos 5 anos, que exclui o efeito das mortes de bebês. Numa sociedade com expectativa de vida de 30 anos ao nascer, ainda pode ser comum que uma criança de 5 anos tenha mais 40 anos pela frente. Ler a média ao nascer como idade típica de morte leva à ideia errada de que quase não havia velhos. Na Inglaterra, estimativas para os séculos XIII a XIX indicam que quem chegava aos 30 anos morria, em média, entre os 50 e os 60 anos.

fontes.titulo: List of common misconceptions about history
fontes.trecho: Adults in the Middle Ages did not die in their 30s or 40s on average, as it is commonly inferred from the life expectancy of the time. While such an estimate was the life expectancy at birth, this was skewed by high infant and adolescent mortality. The life expectancy among adults was much higher; a 21-year-old man in medieval England, for example, could expect to live to the age of 64.

In all pre-modern societies the most common age at death is the first year of life [...] A combination of high infant mortality and deaths in young adulthood from accidents, epidemics, plagues, wars, and childbirth, before modern medicine was widely available, significantly lowers LEB. For example, a society with a LEB of 40 would have relatively few people dying at exactly 40: most will die before 30 or after 55. In populations with high infant mortality rates, LEB is highly sensitive to the rate of death in the first few years of life. Because of this sensitivity, LEB can be grossly misinterpreted, leading to the belief that a population with a low LEB would have a small proportion of older people. A different measure, such as life expectancy at age 5 (e5), can be used to exclude the effect of infant mortality [...] For instance, in a society with a life expectancy of 30, it may nevertheless be common to have a 40-year remaining timespan at age 5. [...] In England in the 13th–19th centuries with life expectancy at birth rising from perhaps 25 years to over 40, expectation of life at age 30 has been estimated at 20–30 years, giving an average age at death of about 50–60 for those (a minority at the start of the period but two-thirds at its end) surviving beyond their twenties.

gancho: Dois símbolos da "Idade Média cruel" não têm prova medieval: a donzela de ferro surge só no fim do século XVIII, e muitos cintos de castidade de museus são tidos como falsificações do século XIX.
explicacao: A donzela de ferro, um armário de metal com espinhos por dentro, ficou famosa com o exemplar de Nuremberg, exposto talvez desde 1802 e destruído num bombardeio aliado em 1945. Alguns historiadores dizem que o escritor Johann Philipp Siebenkees inventou uma história para ela, com uma suposta execução de um falsificador de moedas em 1515 (Siebenkees morreu em 1796). Um professor de história do direito defende que as donzelas de ferro foram montadas com peças achadas em museus, para criar objetos espetaculares de exibição. Com o cinto de castidade, a história é parecida. A lenda diz que as esposas dos cruzados o usavam, mas não há prova confiável de que existisse antes do século XV, mais de um século depois da última cruzada no Oriente Médio. A primeira descrição detalhada é um desenho num tratado militar de 1405, que pode ter sido uma piada. Os cintos expostos no Museu de Cluny, em Paris, no Museu Britânico e em Nuremberg foram em boa parte retirados de exibição porque sua autenticidade como peças medievais passou a ser questionada. O uso mais difundido veio no século XIX, em aparelhos médicos contra a masturbação.

fontes.trecho: The iron maiden is an apocryphal torture device, believed to have been first invented in the 19th century. It consists of a solid iron cabinet with a hinged front and spike-covered interior, sufficiently tall to enclose a human being. While often popularly thought to have been used in the medieval period, there is no known mention of the iron maiden from before the 19th century. [...] Wolfgang Schild, a professor of criminal law, criminal law history, and philosophy of law at the Bielefeld University, has argued that putative iron maidens were pieced together from artifacts found in museums to create spectacular objects intended for (commercial) exhibition. [...] The most famous iron maiden that popularized the design was that of Nuremberg, first displayed possibly as far back as 1802. The original was lost in the Allied bombing of Nuremberg in 1945. [...] Some historians have argued that Johann Philipp Siebenkees (1759–1796) made up a history for the (imaginary) device. According to Siebenkees' colportage, it was first used on August 14, 1515, to execute a coin forger.

According to modern myths, the chastity belt was used as an anti-temptation device during the Crusades. [...] However, there is no credible evidence that chastity belts existed before the 15th century (over a century after the last Middle Eastern Crusade), and their main period of apparent use falls within the Renaissance rather than the Middle Ages. [...] they first became widely available in the form of 19th-century anti-masturbation medical devices. [...] The first detailed actual mention of what could be interpreted as "chastity belts" in the West is in Konrad Kyeser von Eichstätt's Bellifortis (1405), which describes the military technology of the era. [...] Polidoro argues that Kyeser's references are meant to be humorous or ironic [...] Two belts have been exhibited at the Musée de Cluny in Paris. [...] There are other such belts at the Germanisches Nationalmuseum in Nuremberg and the British Museum in London. Most have been removed from public display to avoid any further embarrassment because the authenticity of these belts as medieval devices has since been called into question. Many contemporary historians accept that these alleged "artifacts" date from the 19th century, and are thus inauthentic.

fontes.titulo: List of common misconceptions about history
fontes.trecho: There is no evidence that iron maidens were used for torture, or even yet invented, in the Middle Ages. Instead they were pieced together in the 18th century from several artifacts found in museums, arsenals and the like to create spectacular objects intended for commercial exhibition.

gancho: Segundo a tradição, Ibn al-Haytham fingiu loucura para escapar da ira de um califa do Cairo e, confinado em casa, escreveu o Livro da Óptica, obra que mais tarde seria lida por Kepler e Galileu.
explicacao: Nascido em Basra por volta de 965 e conhecido na Europa como Alhazen, Ibn al-Haytham ficou famoso pela matemática aplicada. Um relato conta que o califa fatímida al-Hakim o chamou ao Egito para controlar as cheias do Nilo. Ele estudou a inundação anual e chegou a desenhar uma barragem no lugar da atual represa de Assuã, mas o trabalho de campo o convenceu de que o plano era inviável. Para não ser castigado, teria fingido loucura. Segundo a lenda, ficou em prisão domiciliar até a morte do califa, em 1021, e nesse período escreveu o Kitab al-Manazir, o Livro da Óptica, datado de 1011 a 1021. Ali ele sustenta que enxergamos porque a luz refletida pelos objetos entra nos olhos, e não porque o olho lança raios, como defendiam Euclides e Ptolomeu, e que a visão acontece no cérebro. Também mostrou com experimentos que a luz anda em linha reta. Para o historiador A. I. Sabra, nessa obra surge pela primeira vez um conceito distinto de experimento. Traduzido para o latim no fim do século XII ou começo do XIII, o livro foi lido por Roger Bacon, Leonardo da Vinci, Galileu, Descartes e Kepler, cuja teoria da imagem na retina partiu diretamente das ideias de Alhazen.

fontes.trecho: Ibn al-Haytham, Latinized as Alhazen (c. 965 – c. 1040), was a mathematician, astronomer, and physicist of the Islamic Golden Age from Iraq. [...] written during 1011–1021, which survived in a Latin edition. The works of Alhazen were frequently cited during the Scientific Revolution by Galileo Galilei, René Descartes, Johannes Kepler, and Christiaan Huygens. [...] According to historian of science A.I Sabra, in Ibn al-Haytham's Optics, "there appeared for the first time a distinct concept of experiment" [...] Born in Basra [...] became famous for his knowledge of applied mathematics, as evidenced by his attempt to regulate the flooding of the Nile. [...] is said to have been forced into hiding until the caliph's death in 1021, after which his confiscated possessions were returned to him. Legend has it that Alhazen feigned madness and was kept under house arrest during this period. During this time, he wrote his influential Book of Optics. [...] In it, Ibn al-Haytham was the first to explain that vision occurs when light reflects from an object and then passes to one's eyes, and to argue that vision occurs in the brain [...] Optics was translated into Latin by an unknown scholar at the end of the 12th century or the beginning of the 13th century. [...] The first theory, the emission theory, was supported by such thinkers as Euclid and Ptolemy, who believed that sight worked by the eye emitting rays of light. [...] Kepler's later theory of the retinal image (which resolved the problem of the correspondence of points on an object and points in the eye) built directly on the conceptual framework of Alhazen. Alhazen showed through experiment that light travels in straight lines [...] This translation was read by and greatly influenced a number of scholars in Christian Europe including: Roger Bacon, Robert Grosseteste, Witelo, Giambattista della Porta, Leonardo da Vinci, Galileo Galilei, Christiaan Huygens, René Descartes, and Johannes Kepler. [...] one account of his career as a civil engineer has him summoned to Egypt by the Fatimid Caliph, Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah, to regulate the flooding of the Nile River. He carried out a detailed scientific study of the annual inundation of the Nile River, and he drew plans for building a dam, at the site of the modern-day Aswan Dam. His field work, however, later made him aware of the impracticality of this scheme, and he soon feigned madness so he could avoid punishment from the Caliph.

gancho: Conta-se que, no saque mongol de Bagdá em 1258, tantos livros foram jogados no Tigre que o rio ficou preto de tinta. A frase mais citada é de um historiador do século XVI, e grandes bibliotecas reabriram em dois anos.
explicacao: Em 13 de fevereiro de 1258, o exército mongol de Hulagu entrou em Bagdá, a cidade dos califas abássidas, e a pilhagem durou uma semana. Entre o que se perdeu estava a Casa da Sabedoria, biblioteca e centro de tradução onde se copiavam obras gregas de filosofia e ciência. Daí nasceu a imagem do Tigre escurecido pela tinta dos livros. A descrição mais repetida vem de um historiador do século XVI, que escreveu que a cor do rio mudou para preto por causa da quantidade de volumes. Uma crônica do mesmo século, de Qutb al-Din al-Nahrawali, fala em livros jogados no Eufrates em número suficiente para formar uma ponte capaz de sustentar um cavaleiro. A historiadora Michal Biran vê nessa frase um recurso literário ligado ao cerco, que ampliava a barbárie mongol, e mostrou que grandes bibliotecas voltaram a funcionar para ensino e estudo até dois anos depois. Bagdá até prosperou sob o domínio de Hulagu, embora tenha perdido peso para a nova capital, Tabriz. A ideia de que esse único episódio encerrou a Era de Ouro islâmica é criticada por historiadores modernos como simplista. E até a imagem da Casa da Sabedoria como uma espécie de universidade é contestada por alguns estudiosos, para quem ela foi construída nos séculos XIX e XX.

fontes.trecho: In contrast to the exaggerations of later Muslim historians, Baghdad prospered under Hulegu's Ilkhanate, although it did decline in comparison to the new capital, Tabriz. [...] Muslim writers have traditionally ascribed the decline of the Islamic Golden Age, and consequently the subsequent rise of the Western world, to this one event; however, such an argument has been criticized by modern historians as simplistic and lazy. Whereas an oft-quoted description from a 16th-century historian details that so many books from Baghdad's libraries were thrown into the Tigris that "the colour of the river changed into black from their multitude," the historian Michal Biran has shown that large libraries reopened for learning and teaching within two years of the siege.

It was destroyed in 1258 during the Mongol siege of Baghdad. [...] More recently, the narrative of the Abbasid House of Wisdom as a major academic institution akin to a university, with specialised departments and organised scholarly debate, has been challenged by some historians, who argue this image was constructed over the course of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries [...] On February 13, 1258, the Mongols entered the city of the caliphs, starting a full week of pillage and destruction. [...] Along with all other libraries in Baghdad, the House of Wisdom was destroyed by Hulagu's army during the Siege of Baghdad. The books from Baghdad's libraries were thrown into the Tigris River in such quantities that the river was said to have run black with the ink from their pages. According to a 16th-century chronicle about the siege from Qu [...] al-Nahraw [...] "So many books were thrown into the Eufrates River that they formed a bridge that would support a man on horseback." According to historian Michal Biran, this quote was a literary trope associated with the siege of Baghdad and magnifying Mongol barbarity. [...] The House of Wisdom included a society of scientists and academics, a translation department, and a library [...] the academy encouraged the transcription of Greek philosophical and scientific efforts.

gancho: A Universidade de al-Qarawiyyin, no Marrocos, é citada como a mais antiga do mundo em funcionamento, fundada no século IX por uma mulher, Fatima al-Fihri. Mas há historiadores que duvidam que ela tenha existido.
explicacao: Segundo a tradição, Fatima nasceu em Kairouan, na atual Tunísia, filha de um comerciante rico. Herdou a fortuna do pai e quis gastá-la numa obra piedosa: uma mesquita em Fez, cujos alicerces teriam sido lançados no primeiro dia do Ramadã de 859. A mesquita virou um dos grandes centros intelectuais do Norte da África islâmico, e a UNESCO e o Guinness a apontam como a universidade ou instituição de ensino superior mais antiga em funcionamento contínuo. Há duas ressalvas. Muitos estudiosos consideram que ela funcionou como madraça, escola religiosa, e só se tornou universidade com a reforma de 1963. E a história de Fatima aparece pela primeira vez séculos depois, num cronista do século XIV, Ibn Abi Zar', visto pelos historiadores como fonte relativamente pouco confiável. Ele conta que a irmã dela fundou na mesma época a outra grande mesquita de Fez, paralelo que o historiador Roger Le Tourneau achou perfeito demais para ser verdade. Numa reforma do século XX, surgiu sob camadas de gesso uma inscrição de fundação em painéis de cedro, que atribui "esta mesquita" a Dawud ibn Idris, filho de Idris II e governante da região, em 877. Com base nela e nas dúvidas sobre o cronista, o estudioso Chafik Benchekroun acha bem possível que Fatima seja uma figura lendária.

fontes.trecho: UNESCO and Guinness World Records have cited al-Qarawiyyin as the oldest university or oldest continually operating higher learning institution in the world. Scholars consider al-Qarawiyyin to have been effectively run as a madrasa until after World War II. Many scholars distinguish this status from the status of "university", which they view as a distinctly European invention. They date al-Qarawiyyin's transformation from a madrasa into a university to its modern reorganization in 1963.

Her story is told by Ibn Abi Zar' (d. between 1310 and 1320) in The Garden of Pages (Rawd al-Qirtas) as founder of the mosque. Since she was first mentioned many centuries after her death, her story has been hard to substantiate and some modern historians doubt her existence. [...] Fatima was born in the town of Kairouan, in present-day Tunisia, possibly around 800 CE. She is said to have been the daughter of a wealthy merchant. [...] When Muhammad al-Fihri died, his daughter Fatima inherited his wealth. [...] The mosque went on to become the most important congregational mosque in Fez and one of the foremost intellectual centers in Islamic North Africa. [...] Fatima did not participate in commerce herself and wished to devote the fortune she inherited from her father to a pious act. She therefore purchased a property in the center of Fez at high cost, where she laid the foundations for the mosque on the first day of Ramadan in the year 245 of the Islamic calendar (859 CE). [...] According to the same tradition, Fatima's sister, Mariam, also founded a similar mosque in the district across the river around the same time [...] Ibn Abi Zar' is also judged by contemporary historians to be a relatively unreliable source. Historian Roger Le Tourneau doubts the truth of the traditional account of Fatima building the Qarawiyyin mosque and her sister Maryam building the Andalusiyyin Mosque. He notes that the perfect parallelism of two sisters and two mosques is too good to be true, and likely a pious legend. [...] One of the biggest challenges to the traditional story is a foundation inscription that was rediscovered during renovations to the mosque in the 20th century, previously hidden under layers of plaster for centuries. This inscription, carved onto cedar wood panels [...] by Dawud ibn Idris (a son of Idris II who governed this region of Morocco at the time) in Dhu al-Qadah 263 AH (July–August of 877 CE). [...] Based on this evidence and on the many doubts about Ibn Abi Zar's narrative, he argues that Fatima al-Fihriya is quite possibly a legendary figure rather than a historical one.

gancho: Uma história famosa diz que o papel chegou ao mundo islâmico por chineses capturados na batalha de Talas, em 751. Mas já se usava papel em Samarcanda décadas antes, e nenhuma fonte chinesa registra a transferência.
explicacao: Em 751, às margens do rio Talas, na Ásia Central, o exército abássida venceu as tropas da dinastia chinesa Tang. Um historiador persa do século XI, al-Tha'alibi, escreveu que prisioneiros chineses tomados ali teriam levado a fabricação de papel a Samarcanda. Para Jonathan Bloom, especialista em arte islâmica e na história do papel, a ligação é improvável. Há fragmentos de papel dos séculos IV e V em Turpan e Gaochang, e cartas em sogdiano dos séculos IV a VI achadas em Dunhuang e Loulan, uma delas trocada com Samarcanda. Segundo Bloom, a cidade usava papel, e provavelmente o produzia, várias décadas antes da batalha. Du Huan, um chinês capturado em Talas que depois voltou para casa, citou tecelões, pintores, ourives e prateiros entre os prisioneiros, mas nenhum papeleiro. Há ainda uma diferença técnica: no século VIII, o papel chinês era feito sobretudo de fibras de casca de plantas, e o islâmico, de trapos, o que sugere uma tradição local mais antiga. Seja como for, o papel se espalhou depressa pelo mundo islâmico: há registros de fabricação em Bagdá em 793 e no Egito em 900. Ficou até uma marca na língua: a palavra inglesa ream, a resma de papel, vem do árabe rizma, fardo.

fontes.trecho: was an armed confrontation between the Abbasid Caliphate along with the Tibetan Empire against the Tang dynasty and its allies in 751. [...] Chinese prisoners captured at the Battle of Talas in 751 introduced paper manufacturing to Samarkand. They engaged in the craft of papermaking while living on land occupied by the Abbasids following Talas. However, this account is unlikely to be factual. Paper was already in use throughout Central Asia by the 8th century; paper fragments dating to the 4th and 5th centuries have been found in the areas of Turpan and Gaochang, and letters written in the Sogdian language between the 4th and 6th centuries have been found in Dunhuang and Loulan. One such letter was a communication with Samarkand. According to Jonathan Bloom, paper was used in Samarkand, and probably produced there, several decades before the battle. [...] By the 8th century, Chinese paper was mostly made of bast fibers while Islamic papers were mostly made of rag fibers. Bloom suggests that papermakers were already active in Central Asia for quite some time and had learned to use rag fibers rather than bast fibers as their primary papermaking material. No historic Chinese source records this transfer of technology through prisoners of war and no contemporary Arabic accounts of the transfer of paper exist.

According to the 11th century Persian historian, Al-Tha [...] Chinese prisoners captured at the Battle of Talas in 751 introduced paper manufacturing to Samarkand. However, there are no contemporary Arab sources for this battle. A Chinese prisoner, Du Huan, who later returned to China reported weavers, painters, goldsmiths, and silversmiths among the prisoners taken, but no papermakers. [...] According to Jonathan Bloom, a scholar of Islamic and Asian art with a focus on paper and printing, the connection between Chinese prisoners and the introduction of paper in Central Asia is "unlikely to be factual". [...] There are records of paper being made at Gilgit in Pakistan by the sixth century, in Samarkand by 751, in Baghdad by 793, in Egypt by 900 [...] the continued use of the word "ream" to count bundles of paper, a word derived from Arabic rizma (bundle, bale).

gancho: Num relato antigo, o sábio Abbas ibn Firnas, de Córdoba, cobriu-se de penas, prendeu duas asas ao corpo, subiu no ar e pousou longe. Feriu o cóccix: teria esquecido que as aves pousam sobre a cauda.
explicacao: Ibn Firnas, que viveu de cerca de 809 a 887 na Córdoba muçulmana, foi inventor, astrônomo, médico, químico, músico e poeta. A ele se atribuem um método para fazer vidro incolor, lentes de leitura e uma técnica de cortar cristal de rocha que dispensou mandar o quartzo para ser lapidado no Egito. O relato mais antigo da tentativa de voo está num manuscrito único de uma crônica da corte de Córdoba, atribuída ao historiador Ibn Hayyan, nascido por volta de 987, e guardado em Madri. Segundo ele, Ibn Firnas vestiu penas presas em seda, com duas asas, subiu no ar perto de Rusafa, deu uma volta e pousou longe do ponto de partida, mas machucou o cóccix por não ter levado em conta como as aves pousam. A pesquisadora Anderson vê nas duas asas sinal de uma asa fixa, capaz de um breve planeio. Já o historiador Richard Hallion acha que ele provavelmente não voou de verdade, mas fez uma espécie de salto de paraquedas com uma capa. Uma versão do século XVII, do historiador al-Maqqari, conta que ele machucou as costas por não ter feito uma cauda. Em 1976, a União Astronômica Internacional deu o nome dele a uma cratera da Lua.

fontes.trecho: 809/810 – 887 CE) [...] was an Andalusi polymath: an inventor, astronomer, physician, chemist, engineer, musician, and poet. He was reported to have experimented with unpowered flight. [...] he lived in Córdoba [...] Abbas ibn Firnas devised a means of manufacturing colourless glass. He invented various glass planispheres, and he made corrective lenses ("reading stones"). [...] he developed a process for cutting rock crystal that enabled Al-Andalus to cease exporting quartz to Egypt to be cut. [...] The earliest known account of Ibn Firnas's flight attempt appears in a unique manuscript of the Cordoban court chronicle al-Muqtabis II, attributed to the historian Ibn Hayyan (born 987/8), now preserved in the Royal Academy of History in Madrid. According to this account, Ibn Firnas covered himself in feathers fastened to silk and fitted himself with two wings, with which he rose into the air; he flew from the vicinity of Rusafa, circled, and landed far from his starting point, but injured his tailbone because he had not accounted for the way birds land on their tails. [...] She argues that the reference to two wings, together with the description of rising and moving through the air, suggests a fixed-wing device, rather than one with flapping wings, capable of lift and a brief sustained glide. By contrast, Richard Hallion proposed that Ibn Firnas probably did not achieve true flight, but rather a kind of medieval parachute drop using a cloak. Some seven centuries after the death of Firnas, the Algerian historian Ahmad al-Maqqari (d. 1632) wrote a description of Ibn Firnas [...] his back was very much hurt, for not knowing that birds when they alight come down upon their tails, he forgot to provide himself with one. [...] In 1976, the International Astronomical Union (IAU) approved the naming of a crater on the moon after Ibn Firas

gancho: No Cairo do século XIII, o hospital al-Mansuri tratava ricos e pobres de graça, usava música como terapia e, na alta, dava ao paciente comida e dinheiro para compensar o salário perdido.
explicacao: Os bimaristãs, hospitais do mundo islâmico medieval, eram sustentados por doações perpétuas chamadas waqf, cujos documentos fixavam as regras: ninguém podia ser recusado por raça, religião, cidadania ou sexo, nem mesmo quem tinha doença mental, e não havia prazo de internação, pois o hospital devia cuidar do paciente até a cura completa. O al-Mansuri, concluído em 1284, foi obra do sultão mameluco al-Mansur Qalawun, que teve a ideia depois de ficar internado num hospital de Damasco, o al-Nuri. O tratamento era gratuito, e o hospital recebia pessoas de todas as origens sociais e religiosas, com mesquita e também capela para cristãos. Assim como o hospital de Fustat antes dele, tratava doentes mentais, e introduziu a música como forma de terapia. Em Aleppo, o hospital Arghun cuidava desses pacientes com luz abundante, ar fresco, água corrente e música. Nesses hospitais, alas masculinas e femininas eram separadas, mas igualmente equipadas, e cada paciente era atendido por pessoal do mesmo sexo. O al-Mansuri ainda funcionava no século XV, e o prédio continua de pé no Cairo. O al-Nuri, que operou por uns 700 anos, também formou médicos: um de seus alunos foi Ibn al-Nafis, o primeiro a descrever como o sangue passa pelos pulmões.

fontes.trecho: Bimaristans served people regardless of their race, religion, citizenship, or gender. The waqf documents instructed that nobody should be turned away; this included those with mental illnesses or disorders. In Aleppo's Arghun Hospital, for example, care for mental illness included abundant light, fresh air, running water, and music. [...] Inpatients were not given a time limit. Instead, waqf documents stated that the hospital was required to care for patients until full recovery. Male and female wards were separate but equally equipped. [...] Patients were treated by nurses and staff of their same gender. [...] Islamic hospitals attained their endowment through charitable donations or bequests, called a waqf. [...] The Al-Mansuri Hospital was another hospital located in Cairo, and was completed in 1284 CE. Its founder, Al-Mansur Qalawun, was inspired to establish a hospital after his own experience being hospitalized in Damascus. Because of Al-Mansur's vision for the hospital, treatment was free to make the hospital accessible to both the rich and the poor. Furthermore, "...upon discharge the patient was given food and money as a compensation for the wages he lost during his stay in the hospital." The hospital also accepted patient of all social and religious background, having both the chapel for Christians and the mosque. [...] Like the Al-Fustat Hospital before it, the Al-Mansuri Hospital also treated mental patients and introduced music as a form of therapy. [...] The Al-Mansuri Hospital remained operational through the 15th century CE and still stands in Cairo today [...] The Al-Nuri Hospital, which operated for some 700 years, was the same hospital where Al-Mansur Qalawun was treated and inspired to establish his own hospital in Cairo. [...] The Al-Nuri Hospital was also a prestigious medical school, with one of its most noteworthy students being Ibn al-Nafis, who would later pioneer the theory of pulmonary circulation.

gancho: Ibn Battuta saiu de Tânger aos 21 anos rumo a Meca, viagem que costumava levar 16 meses. Só voltou ao Marrocos 24 anos depois e, contando as viagens seguintes, teria somado uns 117 mil km, bem mais que Marco Polo.
explicacao: Ibn Battuta partiu em 14 de junho de 1325, filho de uma família de juristas. O nome dele significa "filho do patinho". Pelas estimativas, percorreu uns 117 mil km, contra uns 50 mil do almirante chinês Zheng He e 24 mil de Marco Polo. Nas Maldivas, recém-convertidas ao islã, os chefes locais precisavam de um juiz que soubesse árabe e o Alcorão. Deram-lhe pérolas, joias de ouro e escravos e, ao mesmo tempo, tornaram impossível que ele partisse de navio. Ele virou juiz-chefe, casou-se na família real e acabou deixando o cargo depois de sentenças duras e intrigas políticas. De volta em 1354, ditou suas memórias ao estudioso Ibn Juzayy, por sugestão do sultão do Marrocos. Nada indica que tenha tomado notas nos vinte e nove anos de viagem: dependeu da memória e de relatos de viajantes anteriores. Ibn Juzayy copiou, sem dar crédito, trechos do andaluz Ibn Jubayr, escritos mais de 150 anos antes, sobre Damasco, Meca e Medina, e estudiosos modernos acham que Ibn Battuta não visitou todos os lugares que descreve; há quem duvide até que tenha ido à China. O livro, conhecido como Rihla, ficou desconhecido fora do mundo muçulmano até o começo do século XIX.

fontes.trecho: Ibn Battuta travelled more than any other explorer in pre-modern history, totalling around 117,000 km (73,000 mi), surpassing Zheng He with about 50,000 km (31,000 mi) and Marco Polo with 24,000 km (15,000 mi). [...] "Ibn Battuta" is a patronymic, literally meaning 'son of a duckling'. [...] born into a family of Islamic legal scholars [...] in Tangier [...] On 2 Rajab 725 AH (14 June 1325 AD), Ibn Battuta set off from his home town at the age of 21 to perform a hajj (pilgrimage) to Mecca, a journey that would ordinarily take sixteen months. [...] He would not return to Morocco again for 24 years. [...] However, the leaders of the formerly Buddhist nation that had recently converted to Islam were looking for a chief judge, someone who knew Arabic and the Qur'an. To convince him to stay they gave him pearls, gold jewellery, and slaves, while at the same time making it impossible for him to leave by ship. Compelled into staying, he became a chief judge and married into the royal family of Omar I. [...] these and other strict judgements began to antagonise the island nation's rulers, and involved him in power struggles and political intrigues. Ibn Battuta resigned from his job as chief qadi [...] After returning home from his travels in 1354, and at the suggestion of the Marinid ruler of Morocco, Abu Inan Faris, Ibn Battuta dictated an account in Arabic of his journeys to Ibn Juzayy [...] There is no indication that Ibn Battuta made any notes or had any journal during his twenty-nine years of travelling. When he came to dictate an account of his experiences, he had to rely on memory and manuscripts produced by earlier travellers. Ibn Juzayy did not acknowledge his sources and presented some of the earlier descriptions as Ibn Battuta's own observations. When describing Damascus, Mecca, Medina, and some other places in the Middle East, he clearly copied passages from the account by the Andalusian Ibn Jubayr which had been written more than 150 years earlier. [...] Modern scholars do not believe that Ibn Battuta visited all the places he described [...] Some scholars have also questioned whether he actually visited China. [...] Ibn Battuta's work was unknown outside the Muslim world until the beginning of the 19th century

gancho: No Cânone da Medicina, concluído em 1025, Avicena listou sete regras para testar remédios, como começar pela dose mais fraca e testar no corpo humano, não só em animais. O livro foi ensinado na Europa por séculos.
explicacao: O Cânone, de Ibn Sina, conhecido no Ocidente como Avicena, é uma enciclopédia médica em cinco livros que reunia o saber do mundo islâmico, herdeiro de tradições gregas, persas, chinesas e indianas. O segundo livro lista cerca de 800 substâncias medicinais simples e traz as sete regras, tiradas em parte de Galeno. O remédio deve estar livre de qualidades adquiridas, como calor, frio ou contato com outras substâncias. Deve ser testado numa doença isolada, e não em paciente com vários males, e em duas condições contrárias. A dose deve começar pela mais fraca e subir aos poucos, até não restar dúvida sobre a potência. É preciso observar o tempo que o efeito leva para aparecer. O efeito tem de se repetir em todos os casos, ou na maioria; se não, é acidental. E o teste deve ser feito no corpo humano, porque o remédio pode agir nele de forma diferente do que age num animal. Traduzido para o latim em Toledo no século XII, o Cânone virou livro-texto das universidades europeias. A primeira edição impressa em latim saiu em 1472, e em Pádua ele ainda era ensinado como leitura de apoio em 1715. O médico William Osler o chamou de "o livro de medicina mais famoso já escrito".

fontes.trecho: is an encyclopedia of medicine in five books compiled by Ibn Sina [...] and completed in 1025. [...] It presents an overview of the contemporary medical knowledge of the Islamic world, which had been influenced by earlier traditions including Greco-Roman medicine (particularly Galen), Persian medicine, Chinese medicine and Indian medicine. Its translation from Arabic to Latin in 12th century Toledo greatly influenced the development of medieval medicine. It became the standard textbook for teaching in European universities into the early modern period. [...] Book 2 (the Materia Medica) of the Canon alphabetically lists about 800 "simple" medical substances that were used at the time. [...] The Canon contains seven rules for experimenting with new drugs, taken partly from Galen. "The drug must be free from any acquired quality"; for example from being exposed to heat or cold or stored in close proximity to other substances. "The experiment must done on a single, not a composite condition"; in other words it should not be tested on a patient who has complex or multiple illnesses. "The drug must be tested on two contrary conditions" [...] it is best to experiment first using the weakest [dosage] and then increase it gradually until you know the potency of the drug, leaving no room for doubt." "One should consider the time needed for the drug to take effect. [...] "The effect of the drug should be the same in all cases or, at least, in most. If that is not the case, the effect is then accidental [...] "Experiments should be carried out on the human body [...] the quality of the medicine might mean that it would affect the human body differently from the animal body..." [...] although it was still being taught as background literature as late as 1715 in Padua. [...] The earliest printed edition of the Latin Canon appeared in 1472 [...] William Osler described the Canon as "the most famous medical textbook ever written,"

gancho: No século XI, al-Biruni calculou o raio da Terra sem medir distâncias entre cidades: mediu a altura de um morro no atual Paquistão e, do topo, quanto o horizonte parecia abaixo da horizontal. O resto foi trigonometria.
explicacao: Al-Biruni, que viveu de cerca de 973 a 1050, nasceu em Kath, na Corásmia, e se destacou em física, matemática, astronomia, história e linguística. Para medir a Terra, ele criou um método que pedia só um lugar alto: em Nandana, na região de Pind Dadan Khan, mediu a altura de um morro e depois, do alto dele, o ângulo em que o horizonte aparece rebaixado, a chamada depressão do horizonte. Quanto menor a Terra, mais o horizonte "cai", e a trigonometria liga as duas medidas ao raio. O valor que ele deu foi de 12.803.337 côvados. Quão perto ele chegou do valor moderno depende de quanto media o côvado que usou, e isso não se sabe ao certo: conforme a conversão escolhida, a estimativa fica mais ou menos próxima do raio real. Há um problema mais sério. Al-Biruni não conhecia a refração atmosférica, que curva a luz rasante, e não a corrigiu. Ele usou um ângulo de 34 minutos de arco, e a refração pode alterar esse ângulo em cerca de um sexto, o que deixa o cálculo com precisão de uns 20%. O método engenhoso tinha, portanto, um ponto fraco invisível para a física da época.

fontes.trecho: c. 973 – c. 1050), known as Biruni [...] Well versed in physics, mathematics, astronomy and the natural sciences, he also distinguished himself as a historian, chronologist and linguist [...] Born in Kath in Khwarazm [...] Bīrūnī devised a novel method of determining the Earth's radius by means of the observation of the height of a mountain. He carried it out at Nandana in Pind Dadan Khan (present-day Pakistan). He used trigonometry to calculate the radius of the Earth using measurements of the height of a hill and measurement of the dip in the horizon from the top of that hill. Sparavigna writes that his calculated radius for the Earth of 3928.77 miles was 2% higher than the actual mean radius of 3847.80 miles. His estimate was given as 12,803,337 cubits, so the accuracy of his estimate compared to the modern value depends on what conversion is used for cubits. The exact length of a cubit is not clear; with an 18-inch cubit his estimate would be 3,600 miles, whereas with a 22-inch cubit his estimate would be 4,200 miles. One significant problem with this approach is that Al-Biruni was not aware of atmospheric refraction and made no allowance for it. He used a dip angle of 34 arc minutes in his calculations, but refraction can typically alter the measured dip angle by about 1/6, making his calculation only accurate to within about 20% of the true value.

gancho: No século IX, em Bagdá, três irmãos filhos de um ex-salteador descreveram um flautista automático apontado como possível primeira máquina programável. Os mesmos irmãos levaram o califa a mandar surrar um sábio rival.
explicacao: Os Banu Musa, Muhammad, Ahmad e al-Hasan, eram filhos de Musa ibn Shakir, que na juventude foi salteador de estradas e astrônomo em Khorasan e depois serviu ao futuro califa al-Ma'mun. Órfãos, os meninos foram criados na corte, e al-Ma'mun os pôs na Casa da Sabedoria, onde estudaram geometria, mecânica, música e astronomia. Em 850, publicaram o Livro dos Dispositivos Engenhosos, com cerca de cem aparelhos. Muitos eram jarros de truque para divertir convidados: uma mesma bica podia servir vinho, depois água, depois a mistura. Por trás das brincadeiras havia válvulas automáticas, memórias mecânicas, controle por realimentação e até um sistema à prova de falhas. Eles descreveram ainda um órgão movido a água que tocava com cilindros trocáveis cheios de pinos e um flautista automático, considerado por alguns o primeiro sequenciador musical programável. Ricos e influentes, os irmãos viraram inimigos do filósofo al-Kindi: ridicularizaram seu tratado sobre o astrolábio e levaram o califa al-Mutawakkil a mandar espancá-lo, expulsá-lo da corte e confiscar sua biblioteca. Os livros só voltaram ao dono com a ajuda do estudioso Sanad ibn Ali.

fontes.trecho: One of those inventions includes an automatic flute player that may have been the first programmable machine or computer. [...] who earlier in life had been a highwayman and astronomer in Khorasan of unknown pedigree. After befriending al-Ma'mun, who was then a governor of Khorasan and staying in Merv, Musa was employed as an astrologer and astronomer. After Musa's death, the three orphaned children were cared for at the court of al-Ma [...] Al-Ma’mun recognized their abilities, and enrolled them in the House of Wisdom [...] the three brothers studied geometry, mechanics, music, mathematics and astronomy [...] The inventions employ innovative engineering ideas, such as automatic one-way and two-way valves, mechanical memories, devices capable of responding to feedback, and delay mechanisms. [...] The Banū Mūsā became enemies of al-Kindi, and assisted in his persecution by al-Mutawakkil. They criticized and ridiculed his treatise on the astrolabe, and caused al-Mutawakkil to have him beaten, removed from court, and his library confiscated. The library was returned back to him at a later date with the help of the Persian Jewish scholar Sanad ibn Ali

is a large illustrated work on mechanical devices, including automata, published in 850 by the three brothers of Persian descent, the Banū Mūsā brothers (Ahmad, Muhammad and Hasan ibn Musa ibn Shakir) working at the House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma) in Baghdad [...] The book described about one hundred devices and how to use them. [...] For example, a single outlet pipe in a vessel might pour out first wine, then water and finally a mixture of the two. [...] In modern terms, one would call the method used to achieve this result a fail-safe system.

As early as the 9th century, the Persian (Iranian) Banū Mūsā brothers invented a hydropowered organ using exchangeable cylinders with pins, and also an automatic flute-playing machine using steam power, as described in their Book of Ingenious Devices. The Banu Musa brothers' automatic flute player was the first programmable music sequencer device

gancho: No século XIII, o médico Ibn al-Nafis descreveu o sangue indo do coração aos pulmões e de volta, e previu passagens minúsculas entre a artéria e a veia pulmonar, mais de 400 anos antes da descoberta dos capilares.
explicacao: Ibn al-Nafis, que viveu de cerca de 1210 a 1288, passou a maior parte da vida no Egito e foi médico pessoal do sultão Baibars. Até ele, prevalecia a teoria de Galeno, médico grego do século II: o sangue passaria do lado direito do coração para o esquerdo por poros na parede que separa as cavidades, poros que Galeno nunca viu e supôs pequenos demais. Num comentário à anatomia do Cânone de Avicena, Ibn al-Nafis afirmou que essa parede é espessa e não tem passagem visível nem invisível. O sangue do lado direito, escreveu, segue pela artéria pulmonar até os pulmões, mistura-se ao ar e volta pela veia pulmonar ao lado esquerdo. Ele previu também pequenas comunicações entre a artéria e a veia pulmonar, antecipando em mais de 400 anos a descoberta dos capilares. O manuscrito foi achado em 1924 pelo médico egípcio Muhyo Al-Deen Altawi na Biblioteca Estatal Prussiana, em Berlim. Harvey só publicou seu livro sobre a circulação em 1628. Se a ideia chegou à Europa, ainda se discute: Andrea Alpago, que estudou em Damasco, publicou em Veneza, em 1547, a tradução latina de parte de outro comentário de Ibn al-Nafis, e Harvey chegou a Pádua em 1597. Pode ser só coincidência.

fontes.trecho: 1210/1211 - 1288/1289 CE), known as Ibn al-Nafīs [...] He is known for being the first to describe the pulmonary circulation of the blood. The work of Ibn al-Nafis regarding the right sided (pulmonary) circulation pre-dates the later work (1628) of William Harvey's De motu cordis. [...] Ibn al-Nafis lived most of his life in Egypt [...] He even became the personal physician of the sultan Baibars [...] In 1924, Egyptian physician, Muhyo Al-Deen Altawi, discovered a manuscript entitled, Sharh tashrih al-qanun li’ Ibn Sina, or "Commentary on Anatomy in Avicenna's Canon" in the Prussian State Library in Berlin [...] The most commonly accepted theory of cardiac function prior to Ibn al-Nafis was that of Galen. Galen taught that the blood reaching the right side of the heart went through invisible pores in the cardiac septum, to the left side of the heart [...] However, he could not observe these pores and so thought they were too small to see. [...] The thick septum of the heart is not perforated and does not have visible pores as some people thought or invisible pores as Galen thought. The blood from the right chamber must flow through the vena arteriosa (pulmonary artery) to the lungs, spread through its substances, be mingled there with air, pass through the arteria venosa (pulmonary vein) to reach the left chamber of the heart [...] He stated that "there must be small communications or pores (manafidh in Arabic) between the pulmonary artery and vein," a prediction that preceded the discovery of the capillary system by more than 400 years. [...] In AD 1500, Andrea Alpago returned to Italy after studying in Damascus. In Alpago's 1547 A.D. publication [...] there is a Latin translation containing part of Ibn al-Nafis' commentary on pharmacopeia. This was published in Venice during its rule over Padua. Harvey arrived in Padua in AD 1597. The debate currently turns on whether these events are causally connected or are historical coincidences. [...] The 2nd century Greek physician Galen's theory about the physiology of the circulatory system remained unchallenged until the works of Ibn al-Nafis

gancho: Em 964, o astrônomo persa al-Sufi anotou uma "pequena nuvem" na constelação de Andrômeda. Era a primeira menção escrita conhecida a outra galáxia, mas só nos anos 1920 Hubble mostrou que ela fica fora da Via Láctea.
explicacao: Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi, que viveu de 903 a 986, trabalhava na corte buída de Isfahan, no atual Irã. Seu Livro das Estrelas Fixas, concluído em 964, descreve 48 constelações e compara as estrelas do Almagesto de Ptolomeu com os nomes árabes tradicionais, que pouco tinham a ver com os gregos. Ali aparece a mancha difusa que hoje chamamos de Galáxia de Andrômeda, visível a olho nu em céus escuros; mapas celestes da época a chamavam de Pequena Nuvem. Durante séculos, ninguém soube o que ela era. Em 1920, o chamado Grande Debate, entre os astrônomos Harlow Shapley e Heber Curtis, discutiu se nebulosas espirais como essa eram galáxias independentes. A questão foi considerada resolvida em 1925, depois que Edwin Hubble encontrou estrelas variáveis cefeidas em fotos de Andrômeda feitas com o telescópio Hooker, de 2,5 metros, e com elas calculou a distância. Estimativas atuais põem a galáxia a cerca de 2,5 milhões de anos-luz. Já a ideia de que ele também teria registrado a Grande Nuvem de Magalhães parece ser um mal-entendido.

fontes.trecho: 7 December 903 – 25 May 986) was a Persian astronomer. [...] Al-Ṣūfī lived at the Buyid court in Isfahan. [...] It has been claimed that he identified the Large Magellanic Cloud, but this appears to be a misunderstanding of a reference to some stars south of Canopus, which he admits he did not observe. He also made the earliest recorded observation of the Andromeda Galaxy in 964, describing it as a "small cloud". This was the first galaxy other than the Milky Way to be mentioned in writing. [...] This book describes 48 constellations and the stars within them. Al-Ṣūfī compared Greek constellations and stars as described in Ptolemy’s Almagest with Arabic ones, linking those that were the same. [...] to relate Greek star names with the traditional Arabic names and constellations, which were largely unrelated and overlapped in complex ways.

The Andromeda Galaxy is visible to the naked eye in dark skies. Around the year 964 CE, the Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi described the Andromeda Galaxy in his Book of Fixed Stars as a "nebulous smear" or "small cloud". This was the first historical reference to the Andromeda Galaxy and the earliest known reference to a galaxy other than the Milky Way. Star charts of that period labeled it as the Little Cloud. [...] which place the distance around 2.5 million light-years). Curtis became a proponent of the so-called "island universes" hypothesis: that spiral nebulae were actually independent galaxies. In 1920, the Great Debate between Harlow Shapley and Curtis took place concerning the nature of the Milky Way, spiral nebulae, and the dimensions of the universe. [...] Edwin Hubble settled the debate in 1925 when he identified extragalactic Cepheid variable stars for the first time on astronomical photos of Andromeda. These were made using the 100-inch (2.5 m) Hooker telescope, and they enabled the distance of the Great Andromeda Nebula to be determined.

gancho: Mansa Musa, rei do Mali, distribuiu tanto ouro no Cairo, a caminho de Meca em 1324, que se diz ter desvalorizado o metal no Egito por anos. Na volta, sem dinheiro, ele teve de pedir emprestado a juros altos.
explicacao: Musa governou o Império do Mali no auge, com terras nos atuais Mali, Guiné, Senegal, Mauritânia e Gâmbia. Sua peregrinação, o hajj de 1324, o tornou famoso em todo o mundo islâmico. A caravana acampou três dias junto às pirâmides de Gizé e entrou no Cairo em 19 de julho. Crônicas árabes posteriores falam em milhares de escravos carregando barras de ouro, números que os historiadores tratam como retórica, não como estatística. O dado mais citado vem de al-Umari, que esteve no Cairo pouco depois: antes da visita, um mithqal de ouro valia 25 dirhams de prata; depois, caiu para menos de 22 e não passou disso por pelo menos 12 anos. Há quem diga que isso arruinou a economia do Egito, mas o historiador Warren Schultz argumenta que a variação ficou dentro das flutuações normais do ouro no Egito mameluco. A volta foi menos gloriosa. No caminho de Meca ao Cairo, muitos peregrinos morreram de frio, fome ou ataques de bandidos, e Musa teve de vender bens e tomar empréstimos de mercadores egípcios a juros altos. Segundo al-Umari e Ibn Khaldun, os credores nunca foram pagos ou só receberam parte; outras fontes discordam.

fontes.trecho: was the ninth Mansa of the Mali Empire, which reached its territorial peak during his reign. [...] The Mali Empire comprised land that is now part of Guinea, Senegal, Mauritania, the Gambia, and the modern state of Mali [...] Musa went on Hajj to Mecca in 1324 [...] his hajj, or pilgrimage to Mecca, made him well known across North Africa and the Middle East. [...] Arabic chroniclers writing after the event give widely varying figures for the size of Musa's caravan and the quantity of gold it transported, and modern historians treat these numbers as rhetorical rather than statistical. According to figures preserved in the later Arabic accounts, his procession included upwards of 12,000 slaves, all wearing brocade and Yemeni silk and each said to have carried 1.8 kg (4 lb) of gold bars [...] Shihab al-Din al-'Umari, who visited Cairo shortly after the pilgrimage [...] They camped for three days by the Pyramids of Giza before crossing the Nile into Cairo on 19 July. [...] By the time they reached Suez, many of the Malian pilgrims had died of cold, starvation, or bandit raids, and they had lost much of their supplies. [...] Al-Umari said that before Musa's arrival a mithqal of gold was worth 25 silver dirhams, but that it dropped to less than 22 dirhams afterward and did not go above that number for at least twelve years. Though this has been described as having "wrecked" Egypt's economy, the historian Warren Schultz has argued that this was well within normal fluctuations in the value of gold in Mamluk Egypt. [...] Mansa Musa ran out of money during his journey to Mecca and had to sell property and borrow from Egyptian merchants at a high rate of interest on his return journey. Al-Umari and Ibn Khaldun state that the moneylenders were either never repaid or only partly repaid. Other sources disagree as to whether they were eventually and fully compensated.

gancho: Conta-se que, para escolher onde erguer um grande hospital em Bagdá, o médico al-Razi mandou pendurar carne fresca em vários pontos da cidade e indicou o lugar onde ela demorou mais a apodrecer.
explicacao: Abu Bakr al-Razi, médico persa nascido em Rey, perto da atual Teerã, por volta de 864, estudou em Bagdá e chefiou hospitais ali e na cidade natal. Sob o califa al-Muktafi, que reinou de 902 a 908, recebeu a tarefa de construir um novo hospital, que deveria ser o maior do califado abássida. A escolha do terreno pela carne pendurada é o relato tradicional, hoje às vezes apresentado como uma abordagem baseada em evidências. A preferência por comparar aparece em outros pontos da obra dele. Al-Razi comparou pacientes de meningite tratados com sangria com outros tratados sem ela, para ver se o procedimento ajudava. Também contestou Galeno: as descrições gregas de doenças urinárias, dizia, vinham de só três casos, enquanto ele examinara centenas nos hospitais de Bagdá e Rey. Escreveu ainda um manual de medicina para quem não tinha médico por perto, dedicado aos pobres e aos viajantes. No fim da vida ficou cego. Segundo um relato, recusou a pomada de um médico que não soube dizer quantas camadas tem o olho: seus olhos, disse, não seriam tratados por quem não conhece o básico da anatomia.

fontes.trecho: 864 or 865 – 925 or 935 CE), was a Persian Muslim physician [...] Al-Rāzī studied medicine in Baghdad, where he spent much of his career, and became a successful physician who served as chief physician of hospitals in Baghdad and Ray. [...] It is located on the southern slopes of the Alborz mountain range situated near Tehran, Iran. [...] Under the reign of Al-Mutadid's son, Al-Muktafi (r. 902–908) al-Razi was commissioned to build a new hospital, which should be the largest of the Abbasid Caliphate. To pick the future hospital's location, al-Razi adopted what is nowadays known as an evidence-based approach suggesting having fresh meat hung in various places throughout the city and to build the hospital where meat took longest to rot. [...] His eye affliction started with cataracts and ended in total blindness. [...] Allegedly, he was approached by a physician offering an ointment to cure his blindness. Al-Razi then asked him how many layers does the eye contain and when he was unable to receive an answer, he declined the treatment stating "my eyes will not be treated by one who does not know the basics of its anatomy". [...] For example, he stated that Galen's descriptions of urinary ailments were inaccurate as he had only seen three cases, while al-Razi had studied hundreds of such cases in hospitals of Baghdad and Rey. [...] Al-Razi was possibly the first Persian doctor to deliberately write a home medical manual (remedial) directed at the general public. He dedicated it to the poor, the traveller, and the ordinary citizen who could cons [...] Al-Razi compared the outcome of patients with meningitis treated with blood-letting with the outcome of those treated without it to see if blood-letting could help.
